Retirement spending in phases: separate everyday costs, discretionary plans and later care

Explore four charts that separate changing spending quantities from rising prices, then compare the annual budget with independently indexed net income.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Hypothetical thirty-year category budget beginning at retirement, with year one at the entered starting prices. Essentials increase at general inflation. Discretionary quantity is unchanged for years 1–10, then resets to the selected share from year 11; its prices still increase at general inflation. Additional care starts in the selected year. Its input is in retirement-start dollars, inflated from year one at the separate care price rate, including the years before care begins. Non-portfolio income is entered net and increases at its own assumed rate. Annual funding gap is max(spending minus income, zero). No benefit entitlement, tax, portfolio return, withdrawal order, probability of care, mortality, present value or required starting portfolio is calculated. Surplus income is not saved or carried to later years in the gap total. Care is an additional non-overlapping budget; remove displaced costs separately in a personal plan.

The central idea

A smaller travel budget does not automatically make later retirement cheaper. Separate essentials, discretionary choices and added care, give each a time basis, and compare the resulting cash needs with income.

01

Build a retirement budget from categories and dates

A single retirement spending number is convenient but can hide several different assumptions. Housing and basic food may continue. Travel may change. Additional care may begin later. A category budget lets each event have its own amount, price assumption and date instead of assuming one smooth total describes every year.

The worked example begins at retirement with CAD 36,000 of annual essentials and CAD 18,000 of annual discretionary spending. Its first annual budget is CAD 54,000. Discretionary quantity falls to 60% of the initial level from retirement year eleven. An additional care budget begins in year twenty-one.

These are authored choices for exploring a household plan. They are not survey averages, typical retirement phases or evidence that every retiree spends less on leisure with age. The FCAC retirement-planning guide encourages comparing current expenses with expected retirement needs. The detailed paths here remain independent scenarios.

02

Separate buying less from paying a higher price

Everyday and discretionary prices rise by an assumed 2% a year in the default. Year one uses the starting prices; year eleven has ten increases. The year-eleven discretionary expense is therefore CAD 18,000 × 60% × 1.0210, about CAD 13,165.

The 40% quantity reduction does not mean the nominal amount falls 40% from CAD 18,000. Prices have also changed. Essentials in that same year are about CAD 43,884, making total spending about CAD 57,049 before any added care. In retirement-start purchasing-power terms, the two categories sum to CAD 46,800.

The stacked bars show selected years around the transitions. The nominal-versus-real chart displays all thirty annual budgets and a simple comparison that only inflates the original CAD 54,000. That comparison has no change in discretionary quantity and no additional care. It is a reference path, rather than a recommended spending rule.

03

Give the care assumption an explicit dollar basis

The default additional care input is CAD 18,000 per year in retirement-start dollars. Its assumed price increase is 4% per year from the beginning of retirement, including the years before care starts. When it begins in year twenty-one, the nominal allowance is CAD 18,000 × 1.0420, about CAD 39,440.

Inflating only from the year care starts would use a different meaning: a price quoted at that future date. Mixing those two bases can materially understate a late-life budget. The controls and chart notes specify which meaning applies so the delay does not silently remove twenty years of assumed price increases.

This is an additional, non-overlapping allowance. If paid care replaces housing, food or a family service already in essentials, remove or revise the displaced expense in a personal plan. The calculator leaves essentials intact and therefore does not calculate the net cost of moving into a care facility. It also supplies no care-price quotation, public subsidy estimate or probability of needing care.

04

Deflate consistently when the categories have different price paths

The real spending line divides each nominal annual total by cumulative general inflation. Before added care, the default real budget drops from CAD 54,000 to CAD 46,800 in year eleven. Once care begins, its contribution in those same general purchasing-power units can keep rising because the assumed care price rate exceeds general inflation.

For example, year-twenty-one nominal spending is approximately CAD 108,983. Dividing by 1.0220 gives approximately CAD 73,342 in retirement-start dollars. That number combines the reduced real everyday budget with care whose price has grown faster than the general basket.

The Bank of Canada’s inflation overview explains the role of a broad consumer price measure. A household category assumption is a separate modeling choice. These 2% and 4% paths are constant hypothetical rates, not current CPI observations or an official forecast of personal care costs.

05

Compare spending with the income that reaches the household

Non-portfolio income starts at CAD 36,000 net and rises at an independently entered 2% a year. With the defaults, it matches the essential-spending path. The positive annual gap therefore begins at CAD 18,000, falls when discretionary quantity changes and rises when added care begins.

In year thirty, the annual gap is about CAD 75,315. This is an after-tax household cash need. It is not automatically the gross amount to withdraw from an RRSP or RRIF. The gross withdrawal needed to supply it depends on the accounts, other income, tax and benefit interactions, which this budget model does not calculate.

The sum of positive annual gaps is about CAD 990,497. That is an undiscounted thirty-year cash-flow total, not a required starting portfolio. It assumes no return and does not carry an earlier income surplus into a later year. Estimating starting capital requires an additional model with investment risk, tax, withdrawal timing and the intended horizon.

06

Stress the category that could change the plan

The matrix changes the additional annual care allowance in retirement-start dollars and its price increase, then displays the largest annual spending gap. The care start year and all other selected inputs remain fixed. A darker cell means a larger cash need; it does not describe how likely that need is.

Try reducing the income growth rate while leaving general inflation unchanged. Then move care earlier and test retaining more discretionary activity. Each change answers a different question: income purchasing power, duration of an added expense, or the amount of optional spending. Do not treat an assumed late start as insurance against an earlier event.

Review the plan with actual household spending and confirmed income terms. Identify which costs overlap, what can be adjusted, who would provide support and how receipts might change after a death or health event. Use the related longevity guide for the horizon and the income-bridge guide for the years before later income begins. This article organizes the spending side without claiming a safe withdrawal rate or a universal retirement pattern.
